Triage: `needs-user-decision` + `domain:engine-core` (`packages/objectql` write path) + type Feature. Human floor, not auto-adjudicable: every option changes contract accept behavior — the shipped strict-mode refusal text documents today's "stays locked for every caller" semantics, so options A and B both flip a documented behavior, and option C mints new declared vocabulary. External report with a named downstream customer (titanwind-ehr#1446) and a shipped in-band workaround (#1451), so the reporter is **not blocked** — this is a contract-shape question, not a p0.

## Four-axis card face

1. **Platform long-term coherence**: A shrinks a special case — it gives `stripReadonlyWhenFields` the exact `suppliedValues` discipline the static strip already carries (#5591), collapsing two strip mechanisms onto one accepted rationale. B weakens state locks generally (`isSystem` bypass on the paid-invoice-frozen class #4889 is built on). C is the cleanest contract but the largest new surface.
2. **Measured business pull**: real and specific — a hook-derived, form-visible-but-locked field silently kept a stale value; a scheduler consuming it produced a user-visible duplicate-plans loop, diagnosed only by reading dist. The workaround pattern (predicate token + merged-snapshot read) is exactly what other AI-authored apps will now copy.
3. **AI-agent error-resistance**: today the failure is a silent strip behind an HTTP 200 — the worst shape. A removes the trap for the derived-field pattern. If instead "total lock, hooks included" is confirmed, the card's own fallback is the right floor: spec/docs statement + a publish-time author-rule that loudly rejects an object whose own hook writes a field its always-TRUE `readonlyWhen` will strip (declared-vs-enforced made visible at authoring time).
4. **Startup scope discipline**: A adds no declared surface and reuses an in-file mechanism; C declares a new permanent key; B is one conditional but flips documented wording. A is the cheapest honest move.

**Recommendation: Option A (`suppliedValues` parity), plus doc wording that "every caller" means every API-boundary caller.** All four prisms point the same way, but this is an accept-behavior change on the engine write path ⇒ maintainer's call, and if ruled, the model floor for contract-behavior changes applies (`model: claude-fable-5`).

Fork clause for the eventual implementer: if measurement shows any consumer depends on the strip discarding hook-written values (e.g. as a state-lock guarantee), stop and bring the measurement back — do not route around it.

Dedupe: prior-art sweep in the card body is accurate; no open card covers the hook-derived/`readonlyWhen` gap (checked against the full open set this round).

Triage: this comment comes from the triage seat Routine; not a claim.

**Ruled: Option A — `suppliedValues` parity for `stripReadonlyWhenFields`.**
- The conditional strip gains the exact key discipline #5591 gave the static strip: only engine-entry caller-supplied keys are judged; keys a hook added or overwrote survive. The API-boundary lock is unchanged — a client cannot turn its own key into a "hook-written" one.
- Both by-id and multi-row branches; docs/refusal wording updated so "stays locked for every caller" reads "every **API-boundary** caller".

- **`model: claude-fable-5` mandatory** — accept-behavior change on the engine write path.
- Downstream note: once released, the titanwind-ehr workaround (predicate-token pattern) should be retired per that project's recorded unblock condition — the reporter can be pinged on release.

Label flipped `needs-user-decision` → `pm:queue` in the same stroke.

## ⛔ Dispatch aborted — blocked on the ruling's own model floor. Nothing was implemented; nothing was lost.

PM dispatch seat, session `session_01Y26DJEHSBhhAQ6wwfsHNza`. Following up my claim above.

The ruling makes **`model: claude-fable-5` mandatory** ("accept-behavior change on the engine write path"). I dispatched on that model and the run **terminated immediately on a Fable 5 usage limit**, before the worktree existed. ⭐ **No code was written, no branch was pushed, no partial state exists** — unlike the #9106 incident, where the same limit killed a dev *mid-verification* and work had to be rescued off an ephemeral container.

Label moved `pm:dispatched` → `pm:queue` + **`pm:blocked`**. ⚠️ I am **keeping the assignee** deliberately: another seat picking this up would hit the same wall, and the block is not on the card's substance.

### Why I am not just re-running it on `opus`

That is the obvious move and I am declining it on purpose. The model floor is **a term of the maintainer's ruling**, not a dispatch preference of mine, and the ruling gave a reason for it. Substituting a model to route around a binding term is the same shape as routing around a fork clause.

⚠️ There **is** a precedent, and I want it on the record accurately rather than leaned on: on **#9106** the maintainer's operator authorised finishing on `opus` after the identical limit hit. But that was a **rescue** decision — ~90% of the work was done and pushed, and parking it would have thrown that away. Here the cost of waiting is zero. A rescue precedent does not generalise into a standing waiver, and I am not going to quietly treat it as one.

### What unblocks this — either is fine, whichever comes first

1. **Fable 5 quota recovers** ⇒ I re-dispatch on the mandated model, no further ruling needed.
2. **The maintainer waives the model floor for this card** ⇒ say so on this thread and I dispatch on `opus` immediately.

Everything else on the card is ready: Option A is ruled, the scope is unambiguous, the fork clause is recorded, and the co-tenancy note about PR #9235 touching `packages/objectql/src/engine.ts` stands.

## Second measured attempt on the mandated model — same wall, ~4 hours apart

PM dispatch seat, session `session_01Y26DJEHSBhhAQ6wwfsHNza`. Following up my 07:24Z comment.

Re-dispatched at **11:05Z** on the ruling's mandated `claude-fable-5`. Terminated on the same usage limit, again **before the worktree existed** — no code, no branch, no partial state. Two data points now: **07:22Z** and **11:05Z**.

Back to `pm:queue` + **`pm:blocked`**, assignee still held so no other seat walks into the same wall.

⛔ **Still not substituting `opus` on my own initiative**, and the second failure does not change that reasoning — it strengthens the case for a *decision* rather than licensing me to make one. The model floor is a term of the maintainer's ruling with a stated reason ("accept-behavior change on the engine write path"); a quota being inconvenient is not a finding about whether that reason was right.

⭐ The one thing the second attempt did establish: **this is not a transient blip.** A ~4-hour gap with identical behaviour means "wait for it to clear" is not a plan with a known end, so the card cannot just sit here indefinitely on the assumption that it resolves itself.

**Unblocks on either:**
1. the Fable 5 quota recovering — I re-dispatch on the mandated model, no ruling needed; or
2. an explicit waiver of the model floor for this card — say so here and I dispatch on `opus` immediately.

Everything else is ready and none of it needs re-doing: Option A is ruled, the fork clause is recorded, and the co-tenancy note is now current — PR #9235 has **merged** into `packages/objectql/src/engine.ts`, and #9284 (issue #9154, another seat) is in flight on `packages/objectql`, so whoever takes this branches from current `main` and re-merges before finalising.

⚠️ This card is **not** blocking throughput — I am dispatching other queue cards in the freed slot. It is blocking only itself.

## ✅ Model floor WAIVED for this card — by the maintainer's operator, asked and answered

PM dispatch seat, session `session_01Y26DJEHSBhhAQ6wwfsHNza`. Recording the waiver explicitly so the ruling's written terms and what actually happened stay reconcilable — a ruling term that gets quietly not-followed is worse than one that gets openly amended.

**What was asked:** the ruling mandates `claude-fable-5`; that quota failed twice (**07:22Z** and **11:05Z**, ~4 hours apart), both times before any work began. I put the choice up rather than deciding it: waive and run on `opus`, hold for the quota, or route it to the maintainer on this thread.

**Answer: waive it — dispatch on `opus` now.**

⚠️ **Scope of the waiver, stated narrowly on purpose:** it covers **the model used to implement #9107**, and nothing else. ⛔ It does **not** touch Option A's substance, the API-boundary lock, or the fork clause — all of which stand exactly as ruled. And it is **not** a standing waiver for other cards carrying model floors; the next one gets asked on its own facts, the same way this one was.

Label back to `pm:dispatched`. Re-dispatching now on `opus`, same brief.

⭐ Recorded for whoever reads this later: the earlier refusal to substitute unilaterally was **not** bureaucratic caution — it was that a quota being inconvenient is not evidence about whether the ruling's stated reason ("accept-behavior change on the engine write path") was correct. Those are different questions, and only the person who owns the ruling gets to answer the second one. What the two failures established was that "wait for it to clear" had no known end date, which is what made this worth asking rather than continuing to wait.

## PM answer — **A**, and here is the notice. ⚠️ This change can silently unlock a field on a downstream deployment.

PM dispatch seat, session `session_01Y26DJEHSBhhAQ6wwfsHNza`. The implementer measured a downstream consequence that nobody asked it to look for, flagged it as the PM's call, and ⛔ correctly did **not** contact the downstream project itself. Taking **A**: the notice goes on this thread now, and again at release.

### ⚠️ For the titanwind-ehr reporter (#1446 / workaround #1451) — read this BEFORE retiring the workaround

Your workaround sets a hidden always-locked boolean token in the same payload, and its design **relies on that token being stripped and never persisting**. Under this change that assumption **inverts**:

- the token is written by your `beforeUpdate` hook, so it is now a **hook-derived** value;
- hook-derived values are exactly what this change stops stripping — **so the token now persists**;
- your predicate `!has(record.maint_recalc) || record.maint_recalc != true` reads it from the **merged** snapshot;
- ⇒ a token that starts persisting can **invert the lock on the NEXT update**.

⛔ **The failure is silent and state-dependent.** Nothing errors. The field simply stops being locked on a subsequent write, on records that happen to carry a persisted token. That is worse than a loud break, which is why this is not waiting for the release ping.

⇒ **Before retiring the workaround, check whether the token is still needed at all** — the underlying defect it works around is what this PR fixes — and if you keep any part of it, re-derive the predicate against a snapshot where the token **can** be present.

### Why not B (fold it into the release ping)

The changeset does say *"if an app relied on the strip discarding a hook's own write to a locked field, that write now lands."* ⚠️ **That sentence is true and would not have been enough.** Nothing connects it to their specific token, and a reader who built the workaround on the opposite assumption will read that line as describing someone else's app. The whole point of a downstream notice is that the reader cannot be expected to re-derive the consequence for their own code from a general statement.

⇒ The release ping still happens as the ruling says. This is in addition, not instead.

### On the delivery

⭐ **The fork clause was measured three independent ways rather than waved at**, which is what I most wanted here since it was the one thing that could have stopped this card:
1. a repo-wide sweep found exactly two real `readonlyWhen` declarations, and **no hook writes either**;
2. the pre-fix full objectql suite on unmodified `main` was green apart from the 6 intentionally-red new cases — so **no existing test asserts that a hook-written locked value is discarded**;
3. a downstream consumer sweep, all green.

Any one of those alone would have been an argument. Together they are a measurement, and they are what let the card land rather than bounce back for a ruling.

Also worth recording: **`check:type-check-debt` caught a real defect in the dev's own diff** (objectql TEST_DEBT 355 → 356 — the new pin file called `registry.registerObject()` without its required `packageId`). It fixed the source and left the ledger flat rather than raising the ratchet to absorb its own mistake. ⭐ That is the ratchet working exactly as designed, on the person who added it.

And the reverse verification pinned the right thing: **6 of 14 cases red against unmodified `main`, every one a direction where a hook-derived value should have survived**, while the **8 API-boundary-lock cases passed before and after** — including the laundering case. The lock did not move; only the hook path did.
